nodes.text: The temple of Serapis at Alexandria has, I think, been heard of by everyone, and is actually known to most. The site is raised on high not by nature but by hand and construction, up a hundred steps or more, and extends on every side in vast square spaces; and everything, up to where one comes out at the topmost floor, is built of vaulted work, which, with huge light-openings from above and hidden inner chambers divided off from one another, served the use of various ministries and secret rites. Further, in the upper parts the outermost spaces of the whole circuit are taken up by halls and *pastophoria* (chambers), and by buildings rising to a height, in which the temple-keepers used to live, or those whom they called *hagneuontes*, that is, those who keep themselves chaste. Behind these, too, colonnades set out in square rows ran round the whole circuit on the inside. In the middle of the whole space stood the shrine, raised on precious columns and built on the outside, amply and magnificently, of marble. In it the image of Serapis was so huge that with its right hand it touched one wall and with its left the other: a monster said to have been made of every kind of metal and wood. The inner walls of the sanctuary were clad first with plates of gold, over these with silver, and last with bronze, to serve as protection for the more precious metals. There were also certain things contrived by trickery and art for the astonishment and wonder of the beholders. A very small window on the side of the sunrise was so fitted that, on the day on which it had been ordained that the image of the Sun be carried in to greet Serapis, the timing having been carefully observed, as the image entered, a ray of the sun directed through that window lit up the mouth and lips of Serapis, so that, as the people looked on, Serapis seemed to be greeted with a kiss by the Sun. There was another kind of fraud too, of this sort. The nature of the magnet stone is said to have this power, that it snatches and draws iron to itself. An image of the Sun had been made by a craftsman's hand of the finest iron for this very purpose: that the stone, whose nature, as we said, is to draw iron to itself, being fixed above in the panelled ceiling, when the image had been set in careful balance directly beneath it, and the stone drew the iron to itself by natural force, the image should seem to the people to have risen up and to hang in the air. And so that this should not be betrayed by its quick fall, the ministers of the deception used to say: 'The Sun has risen, so that he may bid farewell to Serapis and depart to his own place.' But many other things too had been built in the place by the men of old for the sake of deception, which it would take too long to list one by one now. But, as we had begun to say, when the rescript had been read out, the crowds of our people were ready to overthrow the author of the error; yet a certain belief had been spread abroad by the pagans themselves, that if a human hand touched that image, the earth would gape open and at once dissolve into chaos, and the sky would suddenly come crashing down. This produced a kind of paralysis in the crowds for a little while. When, behold, one of the soldiers, armed more with faith than with weapons, seized a double axe and, rising up with all his strength, struck the old trickster's jaw. A shout goes up from both peoples; and yet neither did the sky fall nor the earth sink. Then, striking again and again, he hacks at the smoke-blackened godling of rotten wood; when it was thrown down and fire put to it, it burned up as easily as dry wood. After this the head is wrenched from the neck, the corn-measure pulled down, and it is dragged off; then the feet and other limbs, hewn with axes and hauled with ropes, are torn apart, and limb by limb, in place after place, in the sight of Alexandria his worshipper, the decrepit old man is burned. Finally the trunk that was left is burned up in the amphitheatre; and this was the end of Serapis, of empty superstition and ancient error. About his origin the pagans hold differing opinions. Some think him Jupiter, on whose head the corn-measure was placed either because it shows that he governs all things with measure and limit, or that life is supplied to mortals by the abundance of crops. Others think him the power of the river Nile, by whose wealth and fertility Egypt is fed. Some say the image was fashioned in honour of our Joseph, [and of] the measuring out of grain by which he came to the aid of the Egyptians in a time of famine. Others say it is found in the ancient histories of the Greeks that a certain Apis, a householder or a king established at Memphis in Egypt, when grain had run short at Alexandria in a time of famine, supplied the citizens with food in abundance from his own stores; that when he died, they set up a temple to him at Memphis, in which an ox is kept as a token of the excellent farmer, having certain marks of colour, and is called Apis after his name; and that they brought to Alexandria the *soros*, that is, the coffin, in which his body lay, and named it first, by joining Soros Apis, 'Sorapis', and later by corruption 'Serapis'. Whether this is true or nothing at all, God will see to these matters. But let us return to what we began.

There was among them a priest of Saturn named Tyrannus. This man, as if from an answer of the god, used to tell various noble and leading men who were worshipping in the temple, and whose wives had taken his fancy for his lust, that Saturn had instructed him that the man's wife should spend the night in the temple. Then the man who had heard this, delighted that his wife was summoned by the god's favour, would send his wife to the temple, adorned more elegantly than usual and loaded with gifts besides, so that, of course, she would not be rejected for coming empty-handed. In the sight of all, the lady was shut inside; Tyrannus closed the doors, handed over the keys, and went away. Then, when all was silent, he would creep through hidden underground passages up into the very image of Saturn through its open cavities. Now that image was hollowed out from behind and carefully fixed to the wall. And while the lamps burned within the shrine, he would suddenly send forth a voice through the image of hollow bronze to the woman as she prayed intently, so that the unhappy woman trembled with fear and joy, thinking herself worthy to be addressed by so great a god. But after the impure deity had held forth with whatever he pleased, either to cause her greater dismay or to arouse her desire, by some contrivance linen cloths were drawn over the lamps and all of them were suddenly put out. Then he came down and practised upon the stupefied and terrified woman the deceit of an adulterer, with his profane devices. When this had been going on for a long time with all the wives of the wretched men, it happened that a woman of chaste mind shuddered at the deed and, marking things more attentively, recognised the voice of Tyrannus; and returning home she told her husband of the fraudulent crime. He, inflamed with burning anger at the wrong done to his wife, or rather to himself, brings Tyrannus, formally charged, to torture. When he had been convicted and had confessed, and the hidden frauds had been laid bare, every kind of shame and disgrace pervaded the houses of the pagans, as mothers were found to be adulteresses, fathers uncertain, and children bastards. When these things were spread abroad and exposed, the crimes too were swiftly cut down along with the images and the shrines.

And now who could recount the superstitious outrages of Canopus? There, under the pretext of priestly letters (for so they call the ancient letters of the Egyptians), there was an almost public school of the magic art. The pagans venerated this place as a kind of fountain and source of demons, so much so that it drew far greater crowds than Alexandria did. But about the error of this monster too, and what kind of origin they relate for it, it will not be out of place to explain in a few words. They say that once the Chaldaeans, carrying their god Fire around with them, held a contest with the gods of all the provinces, so that whichever won should be believed by all to be God. The gods of the other provinces were made of bronze or gold or silver, or of wood or stone, or of some material that would without doubt be destroyed by fire. And so it came about that Fire prevailed everywhere. When the priest of Canopus heard this, he thought up something cunning. In parts of Egypt earthenware water-jars are commonly made, pierced all over with many very small holes, through which muddy water sweats out and is made clearer and purer. He took one of these, stopped its holes with wax, painted it on the outside with various colours, filled it with water and set it up as a god. And he carefully fitted on top of it a head cut off from an old image, which was said to be of Menelaus's helmsman. After this the Chaldaeans arrive; the contest begins; fire is lit around the jar; the wax with which the holes had been stopped melts; the jar sweats and the fire is put out. By the priest's fraud Canopus is shown to be the victor over the Chaldaeans. Hence the image of Canopus itself is fashioned with tiny feet, a drawn-in neck, and a swollen belly, as if bruised, in the shape of a water-jar, with a back evenly rounded. From this belief he was worshipped as a god, victor over all. These things may perhaps once have prevailed against the Chaldaeans. But now, when Theophilus, priest of God, came, no sweating availed, nor did the fraud hidden under wax come to the rescue. Everything was laid waste and razed to the ground.
